summary: Existing moon simulation software is counterintuitive and filled with excessive features, making it inconvenient and poorly accessible to the public. CraterView makes landing site comparisons intuitive by computing three main factors that dictate a “good” landing spot on the moon (Earth connectivity for direct radio communication with Earth, Sun availability for solar power generation, and physical safety of landing associated with topography and temperature) and computes a numerical “feasibility” score, which is overlayed as a simple heatmap over the NASA-mapped 3D moon model. CraterView extends to a VR interface to let audiences learn through experience and exploration. CraterView accurately forecasts future landing conditions at any given location of the moon, which has been validated to 97% accuracy on NASA LOLA datasets. This lets mission specialists easily identify feasible landing spots in complex areas, such as within the rugged topography of the Lunar South Pole. In summary, our new model is important as it avoids cluttering and takes a simplistic approach that teaches through experience and engagement.
details:
Demo: http://craterview.projectdextera.xyz

Github: https://github.com/Blanwhit/Lunar-Lander-Repo

Imagine you’re a teacher who’s just had a little student, Johnny, in their class ask them why we haven’t landed on the moon in a while.

It is very difficult for children to understand why a site is difficult to land on if you just give them a list of numbers, but you can simplify it to three main categories: you need to see the Sun for power generation, see the Earth to communicate with humans, and land on even ground so your lander doesn’t topple over.

More recently, data from NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) shows that some ridges near the south pole receive near-continuous sunlight, while nearby permanently shadowed craters may hold water ice. However the lunar south pole faces significant challenges due to its very complex topography. Furthermore, current models of the moon possess very cluttered interfaces. These two factors make moon landing mission models inaccessible to the general public, and make analysing these potential missions very tedious and inefficient for mission planners and experts.

CraterView aims to solve these problems by adopting a minimalistic, straightforward, accurate and engaging design. We accomplished this by using the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) dataset from NASA to accurately model a surface replica of the moon with a resolution of up to 5 m per pixel near the poles of the moon, with a lowest resolution of 167 m per pixel. We then added ephemeris data from NASA’S JPL Horizons data to accurately calculate the relative angle and position of the Sun and the Earth respectively to the moon over time. This allowed our algorithm to compute and illustrate the lighting of the moon and the direct connectivity to the Earth. Our model of the Moon’s orientation was cross-validated against JPL Horizons’ own sub-Earth point, and revealed an agreement within 0.45 arcminutes, or 1/150th of a degree, validating the physical accuracy of the model. CraterView also uses Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) data for the Moon’s surface colour and for boulder densities for enhanced graphics of the moon’s surface components and texture.

Once the physical model of the moon was completed, we gathered several key factors impacting the feasibility of landing in moon missions and combined them into a weighted mean for a score. The first criterion was the direct connectivity to the Earth, which is crucial for direct radio communication without relay satellites. We also took the power generation capacity of a point from solar rays, which is fundamental for harnessing energy, illumination, and heat. Lastly, we considered the relative safety of landing based on physical aspects such as slope, surface temperature, regolith density, and elevation relative to the surrounding terrain . These factors are vital for determining whether a mission can successfully land on the moon safely. The three factors were then combined into a metric, labelled the feasibility score. The weighted score is heavily penalized by the worst values of factors, because if a particular location has a very steep slope, no value of the other parameters can make up for it.

The feasibility score is projected onto the surface of the moon. Red indicates that the areas are not feasible to land, while green areas indicate that the areas are feasible to land and satisfy most/all factors. The heat map is an intuitive interface to make the feasibility of each region of the moon easily understood by incorporating the three main factors. This will help mission specialists as it points them to regions where they should be looking and will help the public understand how region feasibility changes over time, so landing is quite complex as you can not land there at any date or time. It is mapped using a piecewise linear utility transfer function, which converts each data input to a score between 0 and 100. Inputs are then combined into categories (Power 25%, Earth connectivity 25%, Landing 50%) and then into a single score using a weighted power mean:

Mₚ = ( Σᵢ wᵢ · sᵢᵖ )^(1/p)

The weighted mean with the p-exponent makes it so that a weak factor can pull down the score even if its weight is small. Any category below a minimum threshold multiplies the score by a further penalty, a knockout such as a slope above 15° sets it to the minimum, and the result is limited to 1–100.

At the poles, a few metres of solar panel height can change how much of the Sun or Earth clears a hilltop. The default score uses a 10 m solar panel and a 10 m antenna. A 0.4° horizon tolerance allows for uncertainty when a body grazes the terrain. It affects the current visibility, time remaining, annual statistics for power and communications. The API also reports the geometry at the requested observer height (2 m by default), without the scoring tolerance.

The model also computes the feasibility score with the illumination of the moon from the years 2000 to 2050. These temporal dynamics allow us to see how plausible sites are for landing over certain periods of time rather than at a specific point in time. Over a prolonged period of time, the feasibility score is highest near the lunar south pole. Particularly, the maximal illumination percentage on the ridge between Shackleton Crater and Gerlache Crater in our model is computed at 81%, while LOLA’s NASA mapping shows a maximum illumination of 80%. This shows that the lunar south pole is indeed an intriguing target for future missions, and also demonstrates viability and consistency of CraterView.

CraterView’s main benefits include the fact that it essentially merges three tools inside of one. The model gives access to a sophisticated map of the moon, the Earth and Sun’s positions, and how physical factors come together to affect mission landing. In current models, this information would be dispersed across many datasets and different websites. Moreover, CraterView gives clear answers to the specific factors it is evaluating, with the option of looking at a more in depth analysis by clicking the “more info” panel. These clear answers are beneficial to both the general public and mission planners, as it reduces ambiguity and confusion. Lastly, our model is made to be accessible for everyone, as it is free and can render quickly without requiring complicated downloading or computational operations.

Our project is creative because users can intuitively understand the difficulty of landing on the moon without being on the moon or learning complex physics or mathematics themselves. We calculate everything for them, such as the feasibility, and the VR physics on the moon. We convert these complex mathematical and physical factors into a comprehensive framework that can be experienced in real time through VR. The implementation of a comprehensive feasibility metric alongside an accurate integrated time-evolving model provides a unique, novel approach that combines both conceptual clarity with rigorous science.

In the future, we aim to continue developing CraterView by incorporating historical data from past landings, enhancing the resolution of the moon, further optimizing the model, and by presenting it to local schools for outreach and feedback.

In summary, CraterView is a moon model constructed simplistically to efficiently and quickly identify moon landing sites. Through a projected feasibility metric and VR interface, the general public can rapidly learn why moon landings are so difficult. Through the more advanced information presented by the “more info” panel, mission specialists can also benefit by quickly understanding why certain landing spots may be ideal and others may be not so ideal during specific times of the year.

CraterView uses:

-Python (data processing pipeline for LOLA/SLDEM2015 rasters and Horizons ephemeris)

-TypeScript and Three.js / WebGL (3D orbital viewer, custom terrain shaders, Web Workers)

-Basis Universal / KTX2 (GPU texture compression)

-WebXR on Meta Quest 2 (with a Cloudflare Worker backend for computer-to-headset pairing and casting)

Apollo Lunar Surface Journal: Apollo 11 landing
NASA NTRS: Lunar Module Landing Gear Subsystem report
NASA NTRS 20260001760: Apollo LM touchdown mass properties
projectRefs: Global Lunar Boulder Map from LRO NAC images (Ben Aussel, 2025, CC BY 4.0)
Poly Haven: Moon Dusted 02 soil material (CC0)
Esri ArcGIS: Lunar LRO LOLA Elevation tile service
